rv.q: Cardinal is a lot of fun until it wears out its welcome.

Chlumsky is also one of the best reasons to see "Cardinal," Greg Pierce's likable if uneven new comedy-drama now playing at the Second Stage Theater off-Broadway.
A broad satire on the current state of American politics, Cardinal amuses, confuses, and infuriates — often, all at once.
Entertaining and wry, it is also meandering and not entirely believable.

But despite the best efforts of the committed and talented cast, director Kate Whoriskey's steadying hand, and Derek McLane's cleverly designed set that allows for near-instantaneous scene changes, Cardinal feels like it was rushed into production far too soon.
Pierce has written a mostly theoretical play about how ideas to help a deteriorating town can take a downward turn but never involves the audience which is its fatal flaw.
Telling a story about urban decay from such a detached and materially comfortable perspective creates an unbalanced work.
Anna Chlumsky (“Veep”) and Adam Pally (“Happy Endings”) bring their formidable comic talents to a new comedy that’s practically devoid of humor.
But, sadly, cardinal red is the only vivid hue on display in an otherwise colorless exercise; Pierce and company end up painting the theatre gray.
All the elements of this production are on the dull side - writing, staging, direction, performance and delivery.

Painting the town red is slang for celebrating in style, but the phrase takes on a decidedly literal meaning in “Cardinal,” a farfetched and muddled play at Second Stage offering little reason to celebrate.
Although there is no real villain in the story, there's no one to really root for either.

cn.t: Critics find this gentrification comedy-drama well-intentioned but uneven, with Anna Chlumsky's performance praised while the script draws fire for sitcom-level dialogue, weak characterization, and a farfetched premise that fails to land.
